questions.q: What is the foundational document that established ASEAN and in which year was it signed?
questions.a: The Bangkok Declaration, signed on 8 August 1967, established ASEAN. A wrong answer (e.g., "Treaty of Amity and Cooperation 1976" or "ASEAN Charter 2008") reveals confusion between the founding declaration and subsequent legal instruments that codified principles or granted legal personality.

questions.q: Explain why ASEAN adopted the principle of "non-interference in internal affairs" as a core tenet of the ASEAN Way, given the region's post-colonial history.
questions.a: Post-colonial Southeast Asian states had fragile sovereignty and diverse political systems (authoritarian, communist, democratic); non-interference prevented external meddling that could destabilize nascent regimes and allowed cooperation despite ideological differences. A wrong answer focusing only on "respect for sovereignty" misses the historical necessity: without this principle, Indonesia (anti-communist) and Vietnam (communist) could never have joined the same organization.

questions.q: Apply the ASEAN Way to analyze why ASEAN has been unable to issue a strong collective statement on the Myanmar coup (2021) despite its Political-Security Community pillar.
questions.a: Consensus decision-making requires all 10 members to agree; Myanmar's junta blocks any condemnation, and members like Thailand prioritize bilateral engagement over collective pressure. Non-interference prevents sanctioning a member's internal affairs. A wrong answer blaming "ASEAN's weakness" without referencing the specific procedural constraints (consensus, non-interference) shows inability to apply institutional design to real outcomes.

questions.q: Compare the economic integration depth of ASEAN Economic Community (AEC) with the European Single Market across four dimensions: free movement of goods, services, capital, and labor.
questions.a: AEC achieves tariff elimination on >99% of goods (like EU), but services liberalization remains partial (positive lists vs EU's negative list), capital flows are liberalized with safeguards, and labor mobility is limited to skilled professionals (Mutual Recognition Arrangements) — unlike EU's full free movement of workers. A wrong answer claiming "AEC is like a single market" ignores the qualitative gaps in services, capital, and labor mobility that prevent deep economic integration.

questions.q: Evaluate the argument: "India's Act East Policy has failed because ASEAN centrality is undermined by great power rivalry (US-China) and ASEAN's own divisions."
questions.a: The argument is partially valid but incomplete. ASEAN centrality is indeed challenged by US-China competition (e.g., competing Indo-Pacific vs BRI narratives) and ASEAN's inability to unite on South China Sea. However, India-ASEAN trade has grown (target $200B), connectivity projects (India-Myanmar-Thailand Trilateral Highway) progress, and India remains a key security partner (naval exercises, capacity building). Failure would require evidence of declining engagement — which data doesn't support. A wrong answer taking a binary "success/failure" view misses the nuanced, multi-dimensional nature of strategic partnerships.

questions.q: Draft a one-paragraph proposal for an "ASEAN+1" institutional innovation that could strengthen ASEAN's collective voice on the South China Sea without violating the non-interference principle.
questions.a: A strong proposal would create an "ASEAN Maritime Code of Conduct Consultative Group" — an informal, non-binding dialogue mechanism under the ASEAN Regional Forum (ARF) where claimant and non-claimant states meet with extra-regional powers (US, China, India, Japan, Australia) to discuss confidence-building measures (e.g., hotlines, joint patrols, scientific research). It respects non-interference by not adjudicating sovereignty, operates by consensus, and leverages ARF's existing inclusive architecture. A poor proposal would suggest a binding dispute resolution body or majority voting — violating core ASEAN principles and guaranteeing rejection.

questions.q: What common mix-up does this lesson flag about ASEAN (Association of Southeast Asian Nations)?
questions.a: Students often conflate ASEAN with the EU, assuming ASEAN has a supranational commission, parliament, and court with binding authority.

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: Student can compare ASEAN's integration model with the EU across at least three dimensions (institutional structure, decision-making, economic integration depth), explain how the "ASEAN Way" shapes its effectiveness in conflict management, and evaluate India's strategic engagement with ASEAN through the Act East Policy.
